captions.instagram:
How does the tongue taste?

The tongue map in your school book is a myth, chilli heat is not a taste at all, and most of what you call flavour is really smell. Open up a 3D mouth, watch sugar, salt and glutamate dock on their receptors, and see why milk beats water after a bhut jolokia.

→ Your tongue is a bundle of muscle covered in thousands of tiny bumps called papillae.
→ Hidden in them are 2,000 to 4,000 taste buds, each an onion of 50 to 150 cells.
→ Five tastes, five receptors: sugar from jaggery docks on sweet, glutamate from tomato dal on umami.
→ Bitter gets about 25 receptors of its own, because bitter often means poison.
→ The famous tongue map is a myth: every part with taste buds tastes all five.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/tongueclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does the tongue taste? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
The tongue map in your school book is a myth, chilli heat is not a taste at all, and most of what you call flavour is really smell. Open up a 3D mouth, watch sugar, salt and glutamate dock on their receptors, and see why milk beats water after a bhut jolokia.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/tongueclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/tongueclear

In this video:
• A muscle covered in taste buds. The tongue is all muscle and no bone, moved by eight pairs of muscles.
• Five tastes, five receptors. Sweet sugars clamp onto T1R2 + T1R3; umami glutamate onto T1R1 + T1R3.
• The tongue map is a myth. A 1901 study found small differences in sensitivity around the tongue's edge.
• Chilli heat is pain. Capsaicin opens TRPV1, a heat sensor on nerve endings that normally opens above about 43 °C, so chilli feels hot.
• Flavour is mostly smell. As you chew and breathe out, aroma flows from the back of the mouth up into the nose.
• Always renewing. Taste cells last about ten days on average and are replaced by stem cells, which is why a tongue scalded by hot tea usually recovers.
